issues.step: Decide to treat: classify the exposure
issues.claim: NCDC 2019: wild-animal bites and all bites in forest areas are category III. Domestic rodents, hares and rabbits do not ordinarily need PEP; forest rodent bites do.
issues.problem: Dangerous omission. NCDC 2019 qualifies the rodent rule in the same document: when the history is unreliable because a similar-looking animal (mole, mongoose) may have been the biter, PEP should always be offered. Mongooses are a recognised rabies source in India (NCDC 2019 introduction; MO module). The NCDC MO module also allows vaccination for bat or rodent bites in unusual circumstances after expert consultation. As written, a casualty doctor told 'a rat bit me' would withhold PEP even when the animal was misidentified.
issues.correction: Append to the point: 'NCDC 2019 (FAQ 13): if the history is unreliable (a mole, mongoose or other look-alike may have been mistaken for a rat), always offer PEP. NCDC MO module: bat or rodent bites in unusual circumstances may be vaccinated after consulting a rabies expert.' Add cite(WB_NGRP, "FAQ 13 (p. 35)") and cite(WB_MO, "§1.7 Table 1 note (p. 18)"). Also add the MO module sentence to the Bats note.
issues.evidence: NCDC 2019, FAQ 13 (printed p. 35): 'Under normal circumstances, rabies is not transmitted by domestic rats. As a general rule, it is therefore not necessary to receive PEP if bitten by a rat ... However, in many cases, the history given by the patient seems unreliable due to similarly looking species such as mole, mongoose etc, in such cases, to be on safer side the PEP should always be offered to the victim.' NCDC 2019 §1 (p. 2): 'dogs are responsible for about 95% human rabies, followed by cats (2%), jackals, mongoose and others (1%)'. NCDC Training Module on Rabies for Medical Officers (https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/resource/1769335160_TRAINING-MODULE-FOR-MEDICAL-OFFICERS.pdf), §1.7 Table 1 note (p. 18): '* Bite by bats or rodents do not ordinarily necessitate rabies vaccination in India. However, bites by bats or rodents in unusual circumstances may be considered for vaccination in consultation with an expert in the field of rabies.'

issues.claim: IDSA 2014: infected bite — an agent active against aerobes and anaerobes, such as amoxicillin–clavulanate 875/125 mg orally twice daily (misses MRSA).
issues.problem: No alternative is given for penicillin (beta-lactam) allergy, and nothing warns that macrolides should be avoided. IDSA's supporting text for this same question lists the alternatives, says to avoid macrolides because of variable activity against Pasteurella multocida, and gives pregnancy cautions (tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones). Macrolides are the usual fallback for penicillin-allergic patients in Indian casualty practice. The preemptive-antibiotic checklist has the same gap.
issues.correction: Add a point: 'IDSA 2014 alternatives (e.g. penicillin allergy): cefuroxime or another second- or third-generation cephalosporin, plus clindamycin or metronidazole if anaerobic cover is needed; or doxycycline, moxifloxacin or a carbapenem. If co-trimoxazole or levofloxacin is used, add clindamycin or metronidazole. Avoid macrolides unless there is no alternative (variable activity against Pasteurella multocida and fusobacteria). Pregnancy: tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones are relative contraindications; co-trimoxazole may be used except in the third trimester.' Keep cite(WB_IDSA, "Q XII; Table 5").
issues.evidence: IDSA 2014 SSTI guideline, Q XII evidence summary (https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/skin-and-soft-tissue-infections/ ; doi:10.1093/cid/ciu296): 'Alternative therapies could include second-generation cephalosporins (intravenously [IV] or by mouth [po]) (eg, cefuroxime, other second- or third-generation cephalosporins), plus anaerobic coverage (clindamycin or metronidazole) if required (Table 5). A carbapenem, moxifloxacin, or doxycycline is also appropriate. If SMX-TMP or levofloxacin is used, anaerobic coverage with either clindamycin or metronidazole should be added (Table 5). Unless no alternative agents are available, macrolides should be avoided due to variable activity against Pasteurella multocida and fusobacteria. Pregnancy is a relative contraindication for use of tetracyclines and fluoroquinolones, whereas SMX-TMP may be safely prescribed except in the third trimester of pregnancy.' (Table 5 itself was not accessible: the OUP full text is behind a Cloudflare challenge.)

issues.claim: timing = "Once, at or soon after the first vaccine dose; not beyond day 7 (NCDC 2019, WHO 2018)"
issues.problem: The day-7 limit is not anchored. Every source counts it from the first vaccine dose, not from the bite, and the protocol drops that wording. A frequent misreading in practice ('no RIG more than 7 days after the bite') would deny RIG to an unvaccinated category III patient who presents late. Two related instructions from the cited sources are also missing. NCDC MO module: RIG can be given at any time if no vaccine has been received. CDC: if RIG was unavailable when vaccination began, it can still be given up to and including day 7.
issues.correction: timing = "Once, with or as soon as possible after the first vaccine dose (day 0); not beyond day 7 after the first vaccine dose, not 7 days after the bite (NCDC 2019, WHO 2018)". Add a point: 'NCDC MO module: RIG can be given at any time if no vaccine has yet been received, so a late-presenting category III patient still gets RIG. CDC: if RIG was not available when vaccination started, give it as soon as it is obtained, up to and including day 7.' Add cite(WB_MO, "§2.3 Mode of administration of RIG (p. 30)") and cite(WB_CDC_RAB, "Common errors — HRIG was not administered").
issues.evidence: NCDC 2019 §2.9 (p. 9): 'RIG is administered only once, preferably at or as soon as possible after initiation of post-exposure vaccination. It is not indicated beyond the seventh day after the first dose of rabies vaccine, regardless of whether the doses were received on days 3 and 7'. NCDC 2019 PEP protocol chart (PDF p. 48): 'Do not give RIG beyond the 7th day after the 1st vaccine dose on day 0.' NCDC Training Module on Rabies for Medical Officers (https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/resource/1769335160_TRAINING-MODULE-FOR-MEDICAL-OFFICERS.pdf) §2.3 (p. 30): 'RIG is more effective if infiltrated immediately or earliest. However, RIG can be administered anytime if the person has not received any vaccine.' WHO 2018 WER 93(16), p. 216: 'Should not be given after day 7 following the first rabies vaccine dose'. CDC Rabies PEP guidance (https://www.cdc.gov/rabies/hcp/clinical-care/post-exposure-prophylaxis.html), Common errors: 'If HRIG was not administered on day 0 when vaccination was begun, it can be administered up to and including day 7 of the PEP series.'

issues.step: Notes (MaternalCollapse.kt: 'India: no MoHFW, ICMR STW or FOGSI guideline…')
issues.claim: India: no MoHFW, ICMR STW or FOGSI guideline on trauma in pregnancy was found (November 2026). Under the UIP, pregnant women receive Td, not Tdap.
issues.problem: Contradiction between files. WoundsBites.kt (tetanus-prophylaxis, step 'Pregnancy' and its note) correctly cites the MoHFW Standard Treatment Guidelines for Management of Trauma 2025 (source tr-mohfw-stg-trauma-2025, already in the app). That guideline has a whole chapter on trauma in pregnancy, which includes a tetanus immunoglobulin command. The source supports WoundsBites.kt. The MaternalCollapse.kt note is wrong, and that protocol's tetanus step leaves out the national TIG instruction.
issues.correction: Replace the note with: 'India: MoHFW STG for Management of Trauma 2025, Chapter 13 (Trauma in Pregnancy), lists "administer tetanus immunoglobulin" (no criteria given) and anti-D 300 µg IM within 72 h for Rh-negative injured patients under definitive care. No ICMR STW or FOGSI guideline was found. Under the UIP, pregnant women receive Td, not Tdap.' Add cite("tr-mohfw-stg-trauma-2025", "Ch. 13 Trauma in pregnancy — Definitive care (p. 59)").
issues.evidence: MoHFW Dte.GHS, Standard Treatment Guidelines for Management of Trauma 2025 (https://www.dghs.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/assets/SwQ7pJMiJepMtqfUQNUJrGOROd584XHIgipqf7gI.pdf). Table of contents: '13 Trauma in Pregnancy'. p. 57: 'Chapter 13: Trauma in Pregnancy'. p. 59: 'Definitive care – ● Administer tetanus immunoglobulin ● Administer 1 ampoule of RH immunoglobulin (300 microgram) intramuscular within 72 hours of injury in all Rh negative injured patients'.

issues.step: Decide to treat: classify the exposure
issues.claim: NCDC 2019: patients presenting months or years after exposure are evaluated and treated as if it were recent. WHO 2018: rabies after 12 months is rare.
issues.problem: Selective quotation. In the same paragraph WHO 2018 says vaccine should always be given when a category III exposure is recognised, even months or years later. It uses the rarity of rabies after 12 months only to allow vaccine to be reserved when supply is limited. Quoted alone, 'rabies after 12 months is rare' reads as WHO arguing against PEP for late presenters, which is the opposite of the source.
issues.correction: '… WHO 2018: always vaccinate when a category III exposure is recognised, even months or years after the contact. Rabies after 12 months is rare, so only when vaccine supply is limited may it be reserved for exposures within the past 12 months.'
issues.evidence: WHO rabies position paper, Wkly Epidemiol Rec 2018;93(16) (PDF via https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/who-wer9316), Post-exposure prophylaxis (p. 214): 'Vaccine should always be administered when a category III exposure is recognized, even months or years after the contact. However, the likelihood of developing clinical rabies declines progressively during the 12 months after the exposure with clinical rabies occurring only rarely after 12 months. If vaccine supply is limited, vaccine can therefore be reserved for suspect and probable rabies exposures that occurred recently or within 12 months.'

issues.claim: WHO 2018: if available, monoclonal antibody products instead of RIG are encouraged; a registry of their clinical use should be kept.
issues.problem: The evidence status is incomplete. NCDC 2019 §9 (cited here) and WHO TRS 1012 both state that WHO's recommendation is for mAb cocktails of at least two antibodies. TRS 1012 identifies the Serum Institute product (Rabishield) as a single mAb, while Twinrab is a two-antibody cocktail. The step presents the two products as interchangeable apart from dose. The licensing year also differs between sources: WHO 2018 and TRS 1012 say 2017, the Lancet 2025 abstract (cited in the Rabishield note) says 2016.
issues.correction: Add: 'WHO TRS 1012 (restated in NCDC 2019 §9 and the MO module): WHO recommends mAb "cocktails" of at least two antibodies. Rabishield is a single mAb; Twinrab is a two-antibody cocktail.' Change the Rabishield note to 'Licensed in India in 2016 (Lancet 2025) or 2017 (WHO 2018, TRS 1012); not in the NCDC 2019 national guidelines'. Add cite(WB_TRS, "§7.8 (p. 53); §8.4 (p. 69)").
issues.evidence: NCDC 2019 §9 (p. 23): 'WHO has recommended the use of Monoclonal Antibodies (mAb) as a "cocktail" containing at least two antibodies against RABV, as alternatives for RIGs in PEP.' WHO TRS 1012 (https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/272364) §7.8 (p. 53): 'WHO has recommended use of mAb "cocktails" containing at least two antibodies against RABV, as alternatives for RIGs in PEP (28). Several human mAbs have been tested against rabies. The first (a single mAb) was recently licensed by the Serum Institute of India (29).' TRS 1012 §8.4 (p. 69): 'A mAb product was licenced in 2017 in India'. WHO rabies position paper, Wkly Epidemiol Rec 2018;93(16) (PDF via https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/who-wer9316) p. 212: 'A single monoclonal antibody (mAb) product against rabies, which was licensed in India in 2017'. Lancet 2025 abstract (PMID 40783290): 'A rabies monoclonal antibody (RmAb) was approved in India in 2016'. Kalita 2025 (PMC12759163): 'TwinRab™, a two-antibody monoclonal cocktail containing docaravimab and miromavimab'.

issues.claim: Lancet 2025 (manufacturer-funded phase 4, 15 Indian hospitals): Rabishield 3.33 IU/kg … Kansagra 2021 (manufacturer phase 3): Twinrab (docaravimab + miromavimab) 40 IU/kg was non-inferior to HRIG 20 IU/kg, with Essen IM vaccine.
issues.problem: The populations studied are not stated, yet the weight calculator will give a dose for any patient. The Rabishield phase 4 trial enrolled patients aged 2 years or older, within 72 h of exposure (24 h for face, neck or hand). The Twinrab phase 3 trial enrolled healthy adults only, with the Essen IM regimen only. Children under 2 (Rabishield), children of any age (Twinrab), immunocompromised patients and ID vaccine with Twinrab fall outside the cited evidence.
issues.correction: Add to the step: 'Trial populations: Rabishield phase 4, patients aged ≥2 years enrolled within 72 h of exposure; Twinrab phase 3, healthy adults on Essen IM only. Outside these groups, the cited trials give no evidence; follow the package insert.'
issues.evidence: Lancet 2025;406:627–635 abstract (PMID 40783290): 'Patients aged 2 years or older with WHO category 3 rabies exposure by a suspected rabid animal were eligible if the exposure occurred less than 72 h before enrolment, or less than 24 h before enrolment for exposures to the face, neck, hand, or fingers.' Kansagra 2021, Clin Infect Dis 73(9):e2722 abstract (PMID 32556113): 'This trial in healthy adults with WHO category III exposure from suspected rabid animal also establishes the safety of TwinrabTM in patients with 1 WHO approved vaccine regimen (Essen).'

issues.claim: NCDC 2019: fingertips, toes, ear lobes, nose, around the eye and genitalia can be infiltrated if excessive pressure is avoided.  [cited only as cite(WB_NGRP, "§2.9 (pp. 9–10)")]
issues.problem: Wrong locator and a missing instruction. Genitalia appear only in §2.6.1.2 (p. 8); §2.9 lists fingertips, toes, ear lobes, nose and around the eye. The same paragraph of §2.6.1.2 also says an infected bite wound is not a contraindication to RIG. The protocol leaves that out, though doctors often withhold RIG from infected wounds.
issues.correction: Change the citation to cite(WB_NGRP, "§2.6.1.2 (p. 8); §2.9 (pp. 9–10)"). Add a point: 'NCDC 2019 and MO module: an infected bite wound is not a contraindication to RIG infiltration.' Add cite(WB_MO, "§2.3 (p. 30)").
issues.evidence: NCDC 2019 §2.6.1.2 (p. 8): 'An infected bite wound is not a contraindication for injection of RIG. Bites on the tips of the fingers or toes, ear lobes, nasal area or external genitalia can be safely injected with RIG, provided excessive pressure is avoided, as this can cause compression syndromes.' §2.9 (p. 10): 'Tip of the finger(s), toe(s), ear lobe(s) or bites on the nose or around the eye can be safely injected with RIG provided the injection is not done with excessive pressure'. NCDC Training Module on Rabies for Medical Officers (https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/resource/1769335160_TRAINING-MODULE-FOR-MEDICAL-OFFICERS.pdf) §2.3 (p. 30): 'An infected bite wound is not a contraindication to the injection of RIG.'

issues.step: Previously vaccinated, immunocompromised and pregnant patients
issues.claim: NCDC 2019: observe 15–20 minutes after vaccination; a previous reaction to a vaccine component contraindicates that same vaccine.
issues.problem: The point stops at the contraindication and does not give the action the sources give: change to a different vaccine product and continue PEP, with adrenaline at hand. A reader may take it as a reason to withhold PEP, which contradicts 'no contraindication to PEP' in the point above.
issues.correction: 'NCDC 2019: observe 15–20 minutes after vaccination. A previous severe reaction to a vaccine component contraindicates that same vaccine: change to a different vaccine product and complete PEP (WHO TRS 1012; NCDC MO module), with adrenaline ready (MO module).' Add cite(WB_TRS, "§8.5 (pp. 69–70)") and cite(WB_MO, "§2.9 (p. 34); Special situations (p. 36)").
issues.evidence: WHO TRS 1012 (https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/272364) §8.5 (pp. 69–70): 'A previous severe reaction to any component of a rabies vaccine is a contraindication for use of the same vaccine for PrEP or PEP, and the vaccine product should be changed.' NCDC Training Module on Rabies for Medical Officers (https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/resource/1769335160_TRAINING-MODULE-FOR-MEDICAL-OFFICERS.pdf) Special situations (p. 36): 'Previous history of severe adverse reaction to ARV: Change the type of vaccine subsequently.' §2.9 (p. 34): 'Following vaccination, the person should be closely monitored and epinephrine should be ready in hand to treat any anaphylactic responses.'

issues.step: Previously vaccinated, immunocompromised and pregnant patients
issues.claim: NCDC 2019: documented complete PrEP or PEP — wound care, no RIG; ID one site, or IM one vial, on days 0 and 3.
issues.problem: Omits the exception printed in the national PEP protocol chart. In a previously vaccinated patient with suspected direct nerve exposure (e.g. deep, extensive bites), the treating physician may consider RIG. The MO module also lists direct inoculation into nerves in extensive deep bites as a cause of PEP failure.
issues.correction: Append: 'NCDC 2019 PEP protocol chart: if direct nerve exposure is suspected, the treating physician may consider RIG infiltration even in a previously vaccinated patient.' Add cite(WB_NGRP, "PEP protocol chart (p. 38)").
issues.evidence: NCDC 2019, 'Rabies post exposure prophylaxis protocol after animal bite' chart (printed p. 38): '**In previously vaccinated individual/s where direct nerve exposure is suspected treating physician may consider RIG infiltration'. NCDC Training Module on Rabies for Medical Officers (https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/resource/1769335160_TRAINING-MODULE-FOR-MEDICAL-OFFICERS.pdf) §2.10 (pp. 34–35): 'Inoculation of rabies virus directly into the nerve in extensive & deep bites.'

issues.step: Decide to treat: classify the exposure (and 'The biting animal: 10-day observation')
issues.claim: Keywords "monkey bite", "bandar ka kaatna"; the only monkey content is "NCDC 2019: the 10-day rule applies to dogs and cats only, not to other mammals such as monkeys."
issues.problem: The protocol is indexed for monkey bites, a common exposure in India, but never says how the sources classify them. The NCDC MO module lists monkeys among animals that occasionally transmit rabies in India. NCDC 2019 treats every wild-animal exposure as category III, and WHO TRS 1012 describes monkeys as wild animals. Separately, 'such as monkeys' in the 10-day point is the protocol's own example: NCDC 2019 §2.2 says only 'mammals other than dogs and cats'.
issues.correction: Add a point to step 1: 'Monkey bites: NCDC MO module lists monkeys among animals that occasionally transmit rabies in India. NCDC 2019 treats all wild-animal exposures as category III. WHO TRS 1012 refers to monkeys as wild animals. The 10-day observation does not apply (NCDC 2019).' Add cite(WB_MO, "§1.5; §1.7 Table 1 (pp. 17–18)") and cite(WB_TRS, "§8.3.2 (p. 65)"). In step 8, write 'not to other mammals (NCDC 2019); this includes monkeys'.
issues.evidence: NCDC Training Module on Rabies for Medical Officers (https://ncdc.mohfw.gov.in/uploads/resource/1769335160_TRAINING-MODULE-FOR-MEDICAL-OFFICERS.pdf) §1.5 (p. 17): 'In India, rabies is transmitted most commonly by dogs and cats (~97%), followed by wild animals (2%) such as mongoose, foxes, jackals, and wild dogs, and occasionally by horses, donkeys, monkeys, cows, goats, sheep, and pigs.' §1.7 Table 1 'Animals transmitting rabies in India' lists 'Monkeys' with the note 'All exposures with wild animals are considered Category III exposures.' NCDC 2019 §2.1 (p. 3): 'Exposures to all wild animals should be treated as Category III exposure.' §2.2 (p. 3): 'The natural history of rabies in mammals other than dogs and cats is not fully understood and therefore the 10 day observation period is not applicable in such animals.' WHO TRS 1012 (https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/272364) §8.3.2 (p. 65): 'Bites of wild animals, particularly monkeys, are normal when people feed them or handle their food and when the animal is threatened, cornered or trapped.'

issues.claim: cite(WB_CDC_RAB, "Vaccine — unvaccinated and immunocompromised patients") and cite(WB_CDC_RAB, "HRIG administration")
issues.problem: Neither locator matches a heading on the CDC page, so a clinician cannot find the text. The CDC statements are under 'PEP for individuals without previous rabies vaccination' (HRIG and Vaccine rows) and 'Patients who are immunocompromised'.
issues.correction: Use cite(WB_CDC_RAB, "PEP for individuals without previous rabies vaccination — Vaccine; Patients who are immunocompromised") and cite(WB_CDC_RAB, "PEP for individuals without previous rabies vaccination — HRIG").
issues.evidence: CDC Rabies Post-exposure Prophylaxis Guidance (https://www.cdc.gov/rabies/hcp/clinical-care/post-exposure-prophylaxis.html, updated 17 Sept 2026). Page sections ('On This Page'): 'Post-exposure prophylaxis recommendations; PEP for individuals without previous rabies vaccination; PEP for individuals with previous rabies vaccination; Contraindications; Patients who are immunocompromised; Care received outside of the U.S.; Common errors when administering rabies biologics'. The HRIG row of 'PEP for individuals without previous rabies vaccination' reads: 'If possible, infiltrate the full dose around any wound(s). Administer any remaining volume intramuscularly at an anatomical site distant from vaccine administration.' Its Vaccine row reads: 'One injection each on days 0, 3, 7, and 14. For those with immune disorders, administer a fifth dose on day 28.'

issues.step: Vaccine and TIG by vaccination history
issues.claim: CDC: unknown history, never vaccinated or incomplete primary series — vaccinate for any wound; add TIG for dirty or major wounds.
issues.problem: No minimum age is given. The step tells the reader to vaccinate any unvaccinated patient, but no tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine dose is given before 6 weeks of age (WHO 2017; MoHFW UIP; ACIP). A neonate or young infant with a wound falls into 'never vaccinated', and the step gives no indication that the vaccine part does not apply. The TIG row of ACIP Table 6 (unknown or <3 doses, dirty wound: TIG yes) still applies.
issues.correction: Add a point: 'Infants: the first tetanus toxoid-containing dose is not given before 6 weeks of age (WHO 2017; MoHFW UIP Pentavalent-1 at 6 weeks; ACIP 2018). Under 6 weeks, the vaccine step does not apply; TIG follows ACIP Table 6 (fewer than 3 doses and a dirty wound: TIG).' Add cite(WB_WHO_TT, "Primary vaccination and booster doses in children (p. 71)") and cite(WB_MOH_TD, "UIP schedule after introduction of Td").
issues.evidence: WHO tetanus position paper, WER 2017;92(6), p. 71 (https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/who-wer9206): 'A primary series of 3 doses of TTCV is recommended, with the first dose administered from 6 weeks of age.' MoHFW UIP Td operational guidelines, 'UIP schedule after introduction of Td vaccine': '6 weeks OPV-1, Pentavalent-1, Rota-1*, fIPV-1, PCV-1*'. ACIP 2018 (MMWR RR 67(2)), Special situations: 'An accelerated schedule can be started as soon as the infant is aged 6 weeks'. ACIP 2018 Table 6: 'Unknown or <3 … All other wounds … TIG Yes'.

issues.claim: WHO 2010: metronidazole preferred, 500 mg 6-hourly IV or orally; penicillin G is an alternative.
issues.problem: A fixed 500 mg dose sits beside a weight-based penicillin dose, with no note that the source gives no paediatric or neonatal metronidazole dose. A reader treating a child may take 500 mg 6-hourly as all-ages. The step also does not mention neonatal tetanus, the form the WHO 2017 paper defines and gives specific supportive care for. For comparison, WHO 2010 does give separate paediatric doses for benzodiazepines.
issues.correction: 'WHO 2010: metronidazole preferred, 500 mg 6-hourly IV or orally (no paediatric or neonatal dose given); penicillin G is an alternative.' Add: 'Neonatal tetanus (WHO 2017: normal suck and cry in the first 2 days of life, then loss of this ability between days 3 and 28 with rigidity or spasms): WHO 2017 adds a dark, quiet environment and nasogastric feeding. The adult doses in this step do not apply.' Add cite(WB_WHO_TT, "Diagnosis; Management of tetanus cases (pp. 58–59)").
issues.evidence: WHO/HSE/GAR/DCE/2010.2, Treatment of tetanus disease (p. 5) (https://iris.who.int/handle/10665/70219): 'Antibiotic treatment: metronidazole is preferred (500 mg every six hours intravenously or by mouth); Penicillin G (100,000–200,000 IU/kg/day intravenously, given in 2–4 divided doses).' Same page: 'For adults, intravenous diazepam can be given in increments of 5 mg … (for children, start with doses of 0.1–0.2 mg/kg every 2–6 hours …)'. WHO tetanus position paper 2017, p. 58: 'The WHO definition of a confirmed neonatal tetanus case is an illness occurring in an infant who has the normal ability to suck and cry in the first 2 days of life, but who loses this ability between days 3 and 28 of life and becomes rigid or has spasms.' p. 59: 'Supportive care should be provided including keeping patients in a dark and quiet environment to reduce the risk of reflex spasms, and nasogastric feeding for newborn infants.'
